How Claude marks AI-generated content
Updated today
• Copy for LLM
Anthropic has signed the EU AI Act's Article 50(2) Code of Practice on Transparency of Al-Generated Content, as a provider of both generative Al models and generative Al systems. This article describes how we're planning to put those commitments into practice, how marking works, and what its limitations are. We'll update this article and publish more detailed technical guidance as it becomes available.
Anthropic's commitments under the EU AI Act's Code of Practice on Transparency of Al-Generated
Content
What our marking commitments mean for Claude:
• New models will mark Al-generated content from day one. Claude models launched in the EU on or after August 2, 2026 will support machine-readable marking at launch. Generated text will carry embedded watermarks, and generated files will include digitally signed provenance metadata where supported.
• Marking works everywhere you use Claude. Marks will apply to output from supported Claude models across Claude Platform (API), Claude, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, and Claude Tag, and wherever Claude is offered, worldwide. Some platforms or features may not support certain marking types.
• We'll help you detect Claude's marks. We'll support users and other third parties to detect Claude's marks, as the Code requires, and we'll share details in forthcoming documentation.
• Existing models are in progress. The law includes a transition period for Anthropic models launched before August 2, 2026, and we're working to add marking support for those models as well.
More details about our marking plans are below.

How Claude marks content
Claude uses two complementary techniques to mark content generated and processed by Claude: (1) watermarks embedded in text, and (2) signed provenance metadata attached to files.
1. Embedded watermarks in text
When a supported Claude model generates text, it weaves an imperceptible watermark directly into the text itself.
You won't see it, and it doesn't change the meaning, quality, or readability of Claude's response.
Because the watermark is part of the text, it will travel with the text when it's copied and pasted elsewhere, and may persist through some editing. Watermarking will be applied at the model level, which means it will be present no matter which Claude product or surface the text comes from.
2. Signed provenance metadata
When Claude generates a supported file type, such as a svg, png, or jpg, it will attach signed provenance metadata.
This metadata follows the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) open standard, which is used across the industry to record information about content provenance. If a signed metadata label is present, it signals that a file was processed by Claude and lets you detect whether the file has been tampered with.
Detecting Claude's marks
We're also working to enable users and other third parties to detect Claude's embedded watermarks and provenance metadata. Detection checks whether a piece of text or a file carries a supported Claude mark. If a supported mark is found, it indicates that the content may have been processed by Claude.
We'll share details on detection mechanisms in forthcoming technical documentation.

record.text: Thank you, @Grok – What is Nonconsensual Intimate Imagery (NCII)? x.com/i/grok/share...

external.description: Nonconsensual Intimate Imagery (NCII)—also called non-consensual intimate images, nonconsensual distribution of intimate images (NDII), image-based sexual abuse (IBSA), or colloquially “revenge porn”—refers to the creation, publication, distribution, sharing, or threat of sharing intimate visual depictions of a person without their consent.  Intimate imagery typically means photos or videos that are sexually explicit, nude, or partially nude (depicting private areas such as genitals, buttocks, or female nipples, or sexual conduct). Definitions can vary by culture and legal context, but the core issue is the lack of consent for the specific act of capturing, altering, or distributing the material.  Key aspects Consent is central and must be affirmative, conscious, voluntary, and specific to the sharing or distribution in question. Consent to create an image (or to share it privately) does not automatically authorize broader distribution. Consent can be revoked. It includes real images, those obtained through theft/hacking/voyeurism (e.g., upskirting), digitally altered images, and AI-generated or deepfake content that depicts someone in an intimate or sexual context without their permission. Motivations can include revenge, control, harassment, extortion (sextortion), profit, or other harms; it is frequently linked to intimate-partner or technology-facilitated gender-based violence, though anyone can be a victim.  Some advocacy groups prefer terms like “image-based sexual abuse” over NCII, arguing that labeling the material “intimate” can understate the exploitative nature of the nonconsensual use.  In the United States, federal and state laws address aspects of this conduct. Examples include civil remedies under 15 U.S.C. § 6851 and the TAKE IT DOWN Act, which (among other provisions) requires certain online platforms to provide processes for removing reported nonconsensual intimate visual depictions (including authentic and digitally forged ones) and creates related criminal prohibitions in defined circumstances.  NCII is widely recognized as a serious privacy violation and form of abuse that can cause significant psychological, reputational, and other harm. Resources such as the Cyber Civil Rights Initiative and platform-specific reporting tools (plus law-enforcement options) exist to help people seek removal and support.
external.title: What is Nonconsensual Intimate Imagery?

An inquest concluded that her workplace environment 'materially contributed' to her decision to take her own life. Moffat died on 20 May 2025 after being informed by senior managers that she had shared sensitive information about colleagues, which she denied. The Treasury failed to follow its written disciplinary policy, which would have clarified that proven allegations would result in a written warning rather than dismissal. During a meeting on 19 May, Moffat was left shocked and upset when she learned the potential consequences of the allegations were unclear. A Prevention of Future Deaths report will be sent to the Treasury, civil service leadership, and Acas to address systemic issues in disciplinary processes and employee welfare. Moffat's family emphasized the need for meaningful changes to prevent similar tragedies, while the Treasury acknowledged the coroner's concerns and stated improvements to support systems are being implemented.

Durch die Eröffnung der offiziellen Website wurde bekannt, dass die Light-Novel-Reihe »Red Riding Hood: A Detective Story (JP: Akazukin, Tabi no Tochū de Shitai to Deau)« von Aito Aoyagi eine Anime-Adaption erhält. Neben dem Produktionsteam und Sprechercast wurde auch der Starttermin offiziell bekannt gegeben. 

Die Ausstrahlung im japanischen TV soll im Laufe des Jahres 2027 starten. Der Anime entsteht bei BENTEN Film und basiert auf den Romanen von Aito Aoyagi. Regie und Drehbuch übernimmt Itsurō Kawasaki (The Yakuza’s Guide to Babysitting), während das Charakterdesign von Manami Minakata und Yūko Yahiro (Kaguya-sama: Love is War) stammt. Die Art Direction liegt bei Izumi Hoki und Hiroshi Katō, das Farbdesign bei Tomoe Yoshimura, die Fotoregie bei Rieko Koike und der Schnitt bei Daisuke Hiraki.

»Little Red Riding Hood« von Yume Miyamoto
»Pinocchio« von Akira Sekine

Futabasha veröffentlichte das Werk im August 2020 als Einzelband. Die gleichnamige Manga-Adaption lief von Januar 2023 bis Mai 2025 und umfasst insgesamt 4 Bände.

Wo andere Angst bekommen oder wegsehen würden, stellt sie Fragen, erkennt Widersprüche und bringt selbst die schlechtesten Täter ins Schwitzen. Denn gegen ihre Neugier und ihren messerscharfen Blick hat kein noch so märchenhafter Plan lange Bestand.
